**AI prompt:** Under Pipeline 1, use the nhanes dataframe, remove rows with missing BMI, IncomeGroup, or Gender, then calculate sample size, mean BMI, and standard deviation of BMI by IncomeGroup and Gender. Sort and print the summary table.
**Verified:** I checked that rows with missing values in those three columns were excluded, confirmed the group counts, means, and standard deviations against the filtered data, and checked the table’s sort order.

**AI prompt:** Arrange the summary table in the order High Income, Middle Income, and Low Income.
**Verified:** I checked that the printed table shows the income groups in that order and that the summary values stayed the same.
## pipeline 1

```{r}
pipeline1_summary <- nhanes |>
	filter(!is.na(BMI), !is.na(IncomeGroup), !is.na(Gender)) |>
	group_by(IncomeGroup, Gender) |>
	summarise(
		n = n(),
		mean_BMI = mean(BMI),
		sd_BMI = sd(BMI),
		.groups = "drop"
	) |>
		arrange(
			factor(IncomeGroup, levels = c(
				"High Income (>3.5)",
				"Middle Income",
				"Low Income (<1.3)"
			)),
			Gender
		)

print(pipeline1_summary)
```

```{r}
nrow(pipeline1_summary)
```

## R Function

```{r}
summarise_mean_sd <- function(data, value, group1, group2) {
  data |>
    filter(!is.na({{ value }}), !is.na({{ group1 }}), !is.na({{ group2 }})) |>
    group_by({{ group1 }}, {{ group2 }}) |>
    summarise(
      n = n(),
      mean_value = round(mean({{ value }}), 2),
      sd_value = round(sd({{ value }}), 2),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    arrange({{ group1 }}, {{ group2 }})
}

r_function_summary <- summarise_mean_sd(nhanes, BMI, IncomeGroup, Gender) |>
	arrange(
		factor(IncomeGroup, levels = c(
			"High Income (>3.5)",
			"Middle Income",
			"Low Income (<1.3)"
		)),
		Gender
	)
r_function_summary
```

```{r}
identical(round(pipeline1_summary$mean_BMI, 2), r_function_summary$mean_value)
```

## Second Function Application

```{r}
weight_by_gender_race <- summarise_mean_sd(nhanes, Weight, Gender, Race)
weight_by_gender_race
```

## Fourth Function Application

```{r}
waist_by_income_gender <- summarise_mean_sd(
  nhanes, Waist, IncomeGroup, Gender
)
waist_by_income_gender

cat("BMI grouped rows:", nrow(r_function_summary), "\n")
cat("Waist grouped rows:", nrow(waist_by_income_gender), "\n")
cat(
  "IncomeGroup/Gender labels match BMI summary:",
  setequal(
    paste(r_function_summary$IncomeGroup, r_function_summary$Gender),
    paste(waist_by_income_gender$IncomeGroup, waist_by_income_gender$Gender)
  ),
  "\n"
)
```

The grouping labels match the BMI summary, and the row count did not change: both summaries have 6 rows. The count could change because the function removes rows missing the selected value as well as rows missing either grouping column.



## Fifth Function Application

```{r}
bmi_by_race_gender <- summarise_mean_sd(nhanes, BMI, Race, Gender)
bmi_by_race_gender

cat("Grouped rows by Race and Gender:", nrow(bmi_by_race_gender), "\n")
```

This produces 10 grouped rows. Each row represents a distinct Race/Gender combination with non-missing BMI, Race, and Gender. There are more observed Race/Gender combinations than IncomeGroup/Gender combinations, so the summary has more rows; combinations with no complete observations are not included.

## Part D: Parity Audit

I compared the R `pipeline1_summary` with the Python `pipeline1_summary` in
`translation.ipynb`.

| Check | R check and result | Python check and result | Match |
|---|---:|---:|:---:|
| Raw row count | `nrow(nhanes)` = 105626 | `len(nhanes)` = 105626 | Yes |
| Column names | `names(nhanes)` = 18 variables listed below | `nhanes.columns.tolist()` = same 18 variables | Yes |
| Missing BMI values | `sum(is.na(nhanes$BMI))` = 9356 | `nhanes["BMI"].isna().sum()` = 9356 | Yes |
| Rows after excluding missing BMI, IncomeGroup, or Gender | `nrow(filter(nhanes, !is.na(BMI), !is.na(IncomeGroup), !is.na(Gender)))` = 87647 | `len(nhanes.dropna(subset=["BMI", "IncomeGroup", "Gender"]))` = 87647 | Yes |
| IncomeGroup/Gender group count | `nrow(pipeline1_summary)` = 6 | `len(pipeline1_summary)` = 6 | Yes |

The column names in both dataframes are `Cycle`, `BMI`, `Weight`, `Height`,
`Waist`, `WeightMEC`, `Strata`, `PSU`, `Gender`, `Race`, `Education`, `Marital`,
`Age`, `PIR`, `EducationClean`, `MaritalClean`, `IncomeGroup`, and `WHtR`.

The rounded summary values match for every group:

| IncomeGroup | Gender | n | Mean BMI | SD BMI |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| High Income (>3.5) | Female | 11743 | 25.74 | 7.51 |
| High Income (>3.5) | Male | 12095 | 26.11 | 6.81 |
| Middle Income | Female | 16432 | 26.39 | 8.20 |
| Middle Income | Male | 15982 | 25.52 | 7.22 |
| Low Income (<1.3) | Female | 16548 | 25.95 | 8.65 |
| Low Income (<1.3) | Male | 14847 | 24.05 | 7.17 |

The R and Python results agree on row counts, variables, grouping labels, group
counts, mean BMI, and sample standard deviation after rounding to two decimals.
